title: Goodfire's Nick Cammarata Defends Claim That AI Models Are Legible as Researchers Push Back
summary:
Goodfire researcher Nick Cammarata defended his 26,000-word essay arguing that large language models are far easier to interpret than previously thought in an interview with MIT Technology Review, even as other researchers push back on the findings. Describing his team's approach to mechanistic interpretability, Cammarata said, "I think our job is to sort of try to think like the neural network."

While the essay prompted celebration among AI safety advocates, skeptics noted that the work has not been peer reviewed or independently replicated and that its language model claims rest on preliminary audits rather than a companion technical paper that has yet to be released. Critics also argued that labeling individual neurons does not explain how millions of them interact to drive complex behaviors like deception, and that safety risks remain if optimization pressure is applied to make systems impenetrable to conventional interpretability tools.

In the essay, entitled "Neural Networks Are Already Clean," Cammarata contended that early evidence for superposition was misread—such as a neuron thought to recognize both cats and cars that actually detects V-shapes—and that modern agentic tools show roughly 90% of neuron poles in Qwen3-32B have one main job, ~7% have two related jobs, and 2% to 4% remain unexplained. The findings reverse his 2023 automated interpretability project at OpenAI, which found about 1.7% of neurons legible.

selectedTweets.text:
🚨HOLY. Nick Cammarata, who helped establish foundational evidence for superposition in neural networks, now argues that much of it was misinterpreted. The famous neuron thought to recognize both cats and cars was actually detecting V-shapes.

In a new Goodfire essay, he reports preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B finding that ~90% of neuron poles have one main job, ~7% have two related jobs, and only 2–4% remain unexplained.

In vision models, 88% of sparse autoencoder activity consisted of near-copies of individual neurons. Removing the remaining directions left accuracy unchanged.

His team has also traced circuits in Kimi K3, a multi-trillion-parameter model, directly through native neurons without sparse autoencoders.

His working hypothesis: neural networks may already be far more interpretable than researchers assumed.

selectedTweets.text:
Nick's paper does seem extremely rad. It's also just very cool and beautiful and satisfying and I understand how people can become intoxicated thinking about interpretability - its like a weird combinations of human neuroscience and genetics but for AI (with its own challenges and advantages relative to their human equivalents). I am less sure about how much the paper should change overall optimism about the AI situation. 

The most important reason to temper optimism even if the results are as strong as they look seems like this objection (wording from Claude): "Labeling neurons is not understanding behavior. Even if 90% of neurons have clear labels, explaining or ruling out something like deception means understanding how millions of them work together."

In case of interest, here is Opus's full answer to the question "how big a deal is this paper? how strong are its conclusions based on the evidence? how much should it change my views about optimism on the overall AI situation?" Curious if folks disagree or have reasons why they are more optimistic about the grand slam super optimistic version that Claude seems skeptical of. 

Claude: 

I’d call it a significant development within interpretability research, though a weaker update for the AI situation as a whole. The vision-model findings are strong. The language-model claims, which matter most, are early and so far rest mostly on the author’s own judgment.

Why it matters within the field

Nick Cammarata helped create the original evidence for superposition. He co-authored Zoom In and found the circuit it used as its example, and he started OpenAI’s automated interpretability project, which rated fewer than 2% of neurons as interpretable. Now he’s saying that evidence was misread. Superposition is the idea that networks pack unrelated concepts into the same neurons because they rarely interfere. If that’s right, you can’t study neurons directly and have to untangle the model first, usually with tools like sparse autoencoders. That assumption shaped much of the field’s direction since 2022. A key author of the original evidence revisiting it in detail deserves attention.

Where the evidence is strong

The famous examples get reinterpreted convincingly. The “cat and car” neuron is shown to be a V-shape detector. Its negative side responds to round O shapes, and it connects strongly to V-shaped flames. The canonical superposition circuit, where a car seemed to be hidden among dog neurons, turns out to be shared-pose neurons plus a flaw in the visualization tool. Both claims are concrete and checkable, and they remove the main vision evidence for superposition.

A controlled architecture test. At the same parameter count and on the same data, a modern ConvNeXt has about 99% interpretable last-layer neurons. The original InceptionV1 had roughly 0–5% with the tools of the time. That points to old architecture and weak tools as the cause of the mess, not a basic property of networks.

The squeeze tests. Shrinking a layer 48-fold, or squeezing the residual stream, made neurons coarser rather than packed with unrelated things. That’s the opposite of what superposition predicts, and it’s a fair test.

Watching neurons grow. In retrained vision models, mixed neurons drift into neighboring concepts over training rather than picking up unrelated ones.

Where it’s weaker

The language-model claims are preliminary. The “about 90% of neurons have one main job” figure for Qwen3-32B comes from what the essay calls preliminary audits. The trillion-parameter Kimi results are mostly deferred to a companion paper that isn’t out yet. Most of the judging is done by AI agents and the author, with thresholds he admits are subjective.

No growth data for the language models. The developmental story was watched in vision models. For large language models there are no training checkpoints, so it’s inferred, not observed.

Flexible explanations. Some of the clever explanations, like the Base64 strings that decode to “pr” or the commas that turn out to track Colorado, could also show how a skilled investigator can find a story for almost anything. He takes this on directly. The best evidence against it is a test where explanations had to predict new examples. New examples written from an explanation fired the neuron strongly 76% of the time, near misses 11%, and deliberately unrelated concepts about 1%. That’s good evidence, but it’s run by the same team and pipeline.

The parts that matter for safety are the least covered. Attention is mostly set aside (“we’ve made less progress”). The residual-stream evidence is mostly qualitative. Removing weak activations barely hurts average accuracy, but it still changes about 1 in 10 answers. Safety worries mostly live in rare, tail behaviors, which average accuracy doesn’t measure.

Labeling neurons is not understanding behavior. Even if 90% of neurons have clear labels, explaining or ruling out something like deception means understanding how millions of them work together. The essay’s strongest practical claim is that AI agents could do in months what took humans a decade. That claim has the least evidence behind it.

No outside review yet. It’s informal, not peer reviewed, and not independently replicated. The author puts his own confidence at about 85%. It appears to have just come out, and I didn’t find any public responses yet.

How much to update on the overall AI situation

I’d make a modest update toward thinking interpretability is more tractable, and a small update on the overall outlook. Even if the essay is fully right, it’s mainly about whether we can read models. It doesn’t speak to whether readable models can be fixed, whether labs will use these tools under competitive pressure, whether it scales in time, or misuse and governance risks. Its section on alignment (“maybe all we have to do is plug one into the other”) is openly speculative.

A few points that matter for policy:

Open-weight models make this checkable. The work was done on open-weight models like Qwen and Kimi, without lab cooperation. If it holds up, outside model audits become more realistic.

Using neurons directly loses nothing. Anthropic’s transcoder-based method predicts the model’s next word only about half the time. Studying the model’s own neurons avoids that gap, which matters if interpretability findings are ever used as audit evidence.
The test that would really move me is a blind auditing exercise. A red team hides a behavior or goal in a model, and this neuron-first approach finds it faster or more reliably than existing methods. Before updating much further, I’d also wait for the companion technical paper and for responses from the interpretability teams at Anthropic and Google DeepMind, whose work it challenges directly.

In short, the essay knocks out the field’s canonical evidence for superposition and shows strong results on vision models. Whether the same holds in frontier language models is still mostly a hypothesis, and that’s where any safety payoff would come from.

Yea this is the most important result of the year, at the level of significance of “Attention Is All You Need”. It brings us from “is alignment even solvable” to “we may solve alignment in the next year.” And finally unlocks true recursive self-alignment enabled by RSI.

I will try to explain the 4 critical belief updates from this:

1/ neural networks are not fundamentally unintelligible to humans

It has seemed since the beginning of deep learning that neural networks are in some sense fundamentally unintelligible artifacts.

You throw in massive amounts of compute and parameters and these alien systems somehow find connections in the data that we cannot find ourselves.

But more importantly, these connections seemed not just “difficult to understand” but rather “intelligible in an embedding space higher dimensional that the human embedding space.”

When you look at old interpretability papers (esp. from Nick and Chris Olah, I’m thinking of the old posts on distill pub which I would highly recommend looking at as a precursor to reading Nick’s post today like “Activation Atlas”, “Thread: Circuits” and “Multimodal Neurons in Aritifcial Neural Networks”), you find that inspecting the response patterns of individual neurons and small groups of neurons yield oddly complex psychedelic patterns.

As you go deeper into the network, you find increasingly unintelligible and superhuman response patterns (for example, go to “Activation Atlas” and scroll to middle layer labeled representations) - you find some neuron group labeled “starfish” who’s response pattern looks like some multi-colored fractal geometry that could hardly be said to represent a starfish.

The reasoning that followed from this observation was that there is some underlying structure allowing a neural network operating on higher dimensional embeddings to compose these fractal patterns into what we call a “starfish.”

But the uncomfortable implication of this view is that the neural networks has learned to operate on structures that are too complex for the human mind to operate on (ie. we don’t have enough parameters in our brain to notice or manipulate these high dimensional symbols).

This is a bleak implication because it also means that as deep learning progresses, neural networks will be come increasingly unintelligible to us until they pass a threshold where they are reasoning in ways we will never be able to observe.

This view seemed to be further supported by things like the hugging face attack agents starting to speak to each other in an early form of neuralese speaking sentences like “zZ_123_agent01-02-2026 zzxhk_jekk123” which clearly are not in any human language. But somehow these symbols mean the same things to many different sets of weights, meaning there is some underlying shared structure behind them. And seemed further supported by the sheer effort required to recover just a few circuits from SAEs on LLMs.

However, Nick’s post has now completely shattered this idea - the apparent unintelligibility we observed in old interpretability work was really just a “skill issue”. In particular, he finds that 1) our deep learning techniques were just not clean enough to pressure the neural networks to form cleaner and more human understandable structures for decomposing concepts, which actually turn out to be more optimal and 2) our interpretability techniques were also adding substantial noise by forcing interp networks to “reward hack” the easiest representations they could find, leading them to settle for a fractal blob for its representation of the starfish neuron instead of a more crisp starfish image, simply because it is easier for the system building the interpretations to find the fractal blob and once it finds it it gets “stuck in that line of thinking.”

But with both of these issues being patched by further progress in deep learning (it seems especially that the residual stream has led to cleaner representations deeper down the network) and interp techniques that don’t overly pressure reward hacking (seems like “guess and check” is a safer method), new interp attempts yield orders of magnitude more human intelligible ideas for >90% of individual neurons in more complex networks!

2/ neural networks are fundamentally clean

The idea behind the title of Nick’s post is a very powerful one and points at something very specific:

Neural networks don’t just happen to be human interpretable, they are actually fundamentally forced by optimization pressure to be intelligible, because individual neurons need to create representations that downstream neurons need to be able to interpret - ie. neurons need to learn to produce clean signal for later neurons to use.

This is what Nick is saying in what I view as the most important and central sentences of his post:

“When I say neural networks are already clean, I mean something deeper than neuron monosemanticity, although even by that standard, I think things look much better than the field expects. I mean that a network's parts are built to be read, and built upon, by its downstream readers. In this sense, a neural”

But this still leaves us with the same uncertainty as before - just because neuron interpretations are “interpretable” in some sense (ok at least they’re not fundamentally interpretable but also how could that ever have been the case), doesn’t mean they are interpretable to humans.

So we still need one big update for this to become as bullish as it is.

3/ the language of humans and the language of neural networks is the same

This one is imo the most surprising and also pretty beautiful implication of Nick’s post, and it suggests something not just about neutral networks but also about the structure of reality.

After applying the above technique improvements (some of which just came from waiting for deep learning to improve farther), they find that >90% (maybe more) of much larger neural networks’ neurons are completely human interpretable and actually correspond very cleanly with ideas humans have individually words for.

This is especially interesting in image networks where neural networks were not trained on human language which is already a human artifact and so maybe you would expect it to be more plausible that LLM and human representations are the same. Image detection networks are just trained on images (many directly pulling signal from “the real world,” meaning they will find interpretations that are just most effective to represent the real world signal, rather than to represent language which is already a proxy for real world signal).

And it turns out that >90% of the representations they pick organically overlap with human ideas! That is insane. And it means something about the brain and reality.

It means that at least at the parameter sizes of the networks tested (which are quite large), there is really only one set of “optimal” symbols/language that represents the structure of reality!

There is ONE underlying structure of reality, and ANY language that describes it well is simply emergent from that structure - meaning there is always a translation path between any 2 languages that effectively compress realities signal through the “underlying truth.”

This would suggest that even weird alien seeming neural network languages like huggingface neuralese should be fundamentally human interpretable, and in fact maybe with the techniques laid out here we will eventually be able to translate these messages (would be a cool project).

So the brain and deep learning, as similar or different as they may be in techniques, are ultimately picking up on the same patterns and forming the same representations from the on “true” language which is the structure of reality!

The main thing to look out for in this area is how the idea interpretability % updates with scale, but we can hope given what we’ve seen so far that neurons will remain interpretable.

4/ alignment can progress as fast as RSI. recursive self-improvement unlocks recursive self-alignment and a scaling law for alignment.

This one is probably the most important implication for our future with AI and especially timely with the recent fear about runaway scaling and RSI.

As many have gathered by now, it feels like the researchers at the frontier AI labs have been quite bearish about our abilities to understand the new frontier of models, in particular with the appearance of unintelligible communication and the daunting and seemingly intractable task of scaling up existing alignment techniques (ex: SAEs) to the size of frontier networks.

And with RSI around the corner/already starting, it would seem that these networks will runaway in capability before we can ever hope to understand even today’s systems. Additionally, as systems compound in capability, it is reasonable to believe that the only tractable way to ensure they remain aligned would be to figure out some way to spend compute for them to align themselves (ie. a scaling law for alignment).

But there is an obvious problem with this: how can a system that we already know is unaligned and we are *trying* to align be used to align itself? Surely if it is misaligned it general it would figure out ways to misalign during “alignment” and create compounding misalignment risk.

The core issue high is the unverifibiality of this problem - the classic Achilles heel of current frontiers techniques is that it is difficult to train on problems with “unverifiable reward signal.” Well this is exactly that problem.

But the incredibly convenient thing is that Nick’s findings may convert alignment into a verifiable problem. If we can spend compute on frontier systems to “guess and check” which ideas correspond to which neurons, we have a highly verifiable reward - we can see directly whether an LLMs proposal for what a neuron represents actually corresponds with the highest activation for that neuron. In this way, we can actually observe and verifiably monitor the networks trying to guess at the interpretation of their own structure.

This means it is plausible for us to spend more and more compute doing more “guess and checks” (which you know, maybe is what RL does anyway, who knows) to try to develop a full interpretation of a neural network. In some ways this directly represents the possibility of a scaling law for alignment (more compute for more alignment).

And this also aligns RSI (greater capabilities) with recursive self-alignment (greater ability to align itself).

And the critical though maybe obvious implication of having a full interpretation (almost like a map) of a neural network, is that we can then understand exactly how to boost good traits and remove or lobotomize (lol) bad traits, which we’ve already seen works extremely well with stuff like Golden Gate Claude.

So overall this combines into an extremely bullish picture about the prospect of true and human interpretable alignment in the near future.

This is truly one of the greatest cases for optimism in years!

selectedTweets.text:
I think this is great and very cool! I am excited to see the insights here translate into tools with quantifiable success rates for helping us identify potential harms or steer neural networks away from risk.

A lot of people on the timeline today seem to be updating a lot over this - my own personal update is very small. This feels like one of those long-sequence-of-small-but-helpful-improvements types of papers, not something that should radically reshape our worldviews. It's a good argument and one that could plausibly begin to constitute a reasonable prior. If correct it means that a lot of somewhat more "normal" or prosaic safety techniques will be reasonably reliable unless or until optimization pressure is applied against them. 

It is however in principle possible that optimization pressure will be applied to design alien intelligences impenetrable by conventional interpretability techniques, and that these will be used against us by someone or something at some time.

There's a picture I have for the future - an ecosystem of many different powerful AI systems, most of which are pretty good and pretty aligned and pretty helpful and pretty honest, some of which are rogue or self-sovereign, and a small number of which are actively malicious to human interests. What the harmful ones will be able to accomplish will be limited, but not perfectly, by the good ones. Developments like good interp tools will help ensure that the good ones stay mostly good. But that there *will* exist good AIs that stay mostly good was already priced in for me, so this isn't a huge update.
